Making Rubber Reliable

Natural rubber begins as latex, a milky liquid produced by certain plants. Latex contains tiny rubber particles suspended in water, when the liquid is collected and treated, those particles can join into a flexible solid.[1] As water is removed, the particles congregate[2] into a continuous mass. The resulting material stretches and resists water, qualities that made it useful long before industrial manufacturing.

Communities in Mesoamerica learned to process latex into durable objects, including balls and water-resistant goods. These uses show that rubber technology did not begin with nineteenth-century European factories.[3] When European manufacturers later obtained natural rubber, they tried to adapt their[4] unusual properties to shoes, coats, and containers.

The material presented a stubborn problem. Untreated rubber softened and became sticky in hot weather, while cold temperatures made it stiff. In contrast,[5] an object that worked well in one season might become unusable in another. During the early nineteenth century, manufacturers experiment[6] with powders, solvents, and surface coatings in order to be able to[7] make rubber more stable. The long molecules can also move enough for untreated rubber to stretch and partly regain its shape.

Heating rubber with sulfur produced a more dependable result, the treated material remained elastic across a wider range of temperatures.[8] Heat helps sulfur form links between long rubber molecules. Those links limit how freely the molecules can slide past one another, reducing both stickiness and brittleness.

[A] The process became known as vulcanization. [B] Manufacturers could adjust the treatment for products requiring different degrees of flexibility and strength.[9] [C] Softer rubber could cushion moving parts, while harder formulations could support rigid objects. [D] Later improvements made production more consistent and expanded the range of useful rubber goods.

Vulcanization did not create the useful qualities of natural rubber; it made those qualities dependable under more conditions. By overcoming the material's sensitivity to temperature, the process helped transform rubber from a difficult raw substance into a practical component of belts, seals, hoses, tires, and countless other products.[10]
